country.comment: Macro urban water coverage analysis covers urban Kenya (including Nairobi, Kirinyaga, Kwale, and Nithi WSPs), and primary field investigation was conducted in the Mathare informal settlement in Nairobi, Kenya.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title & Abstract; PDF pp. 3-4, Materials and methods; PDF p. 5, Access to safe water in urban Kenya: the macro trends

effect_estimate.comment: Combines secondary regulatory coverage trends with primary survey statistics (N = 258 households in Mathare, Tables 1-3) and qualitative institutional findings; no multivariable regression or causal treatment effect is estimated.
effect_estimate.value: Secondary WSRB data indicate reported piped water coverage in Nairobi rose to 66% in 2007 and increased by about 15 percentage points between 2007-2008 and 2014-2015 to reach 80% (versus 55% average across urban Kenya; Figure 1), largely via counting communal standpipes/yard connections and metering informal-settlement connections, though likely inflated by dormant connections and non-mandatory disaggregate low-income area reporting. In primary surveys of 258 standpipe-reliant households in Mathare (2016-2017; ~88% of slum dwellers use standpipes), weak enforcement of licensed bulk tariff contracts (utility bulk rate Ksh 30 / USD 0.30 per m3; prepaid water ATM rate Ksh 2.50 / USD 0.025 per m3 or Ksh 0.5 per 20L) and unlicensed resellers paying progressive domestic block tariffs (Ksh 64 / USD 0.64 per m3) resulted in elevated, arbitrary consumer prices: 51.90% (134/258) paid Ksh 0.15/L (Ksh 3 per 20L jerry can; estimated 80% operator profit), 24% (62/258) paid Ksh 0.15-0.25/L (80-88% profit), and 4.70% (12/258) paid Ksh 0.15-0.50/L (80-94% profit), with scarcity spikes reaching Ksh 10-15 per 20L jerry can and vendor prices reaching Ksh 150-200/m3 (Tables 1-2). Overcrowded standpipes (averaging 315 users vs. 250 prescribed threshold), erratic supply hours, political/tribal patronage in operator licensing and queue/price favouritism, and cartel vandalism of water ATMs further restricted access. Overall, 83.7% (216/258) of surveyed households reported not being able to pay more for improved services (including 87.5% [56/64, p < 0.01] of poor and 87.7% [100/114, p < 0.01] of lower-class households) and only 4.7% (12/258) were willing to pay (Table 3); moreover, ambiguous land ownership prevents the utility from extending individual household connections even where residents can pay.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Mixed-methods case study (design ceiling = 2) that directly observes and documents the operation of licensing/bulk-tariff contracts, progressive block tariffs on unlicensed operators, prepaid water ATMs, operator discretion/tribal patronage, and tenure barriers to household connections in Mathare.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines ambiguous land ownership/tenure and colonial racial zoning blocking individual household connections (ELIGIBILITY: tenure, property, zoning, planning); standpipe resale tariffs, bulk vs. block tariffs, and ability to pay (BURDEN: fees); operator discretion in arbitrary price hikes and tribal/vendor queue favouritism, community/SHG/CBO management, and low-cost kiosk/prepaid ATM/licensed reseller accommodations (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: discretion, accommodation, participation); and lax enforcement of licensed resale contracts, non-mandatory LIA reporting, consumer complaints/Water Appeals Board, and unpoliced illegal connections/cartel vandalism (ENFORCEMENT: sanction, complaint).
